utterances.text: Ms. Selmani, the accused asked you whether you thought it was possible that the men who you last saw in that meadow at Meja had been released and joined the KLA or had been killed in the bombing. My question for you is this: On the 27th of April, 1999, as you passed that meadow near Meja and you saw your relatives being beaten as they ran up towards the meadow, and forced to squat down there, did you see or did you hear any bombs falling?

utterances.speaker: MERFIDETE SELMANI
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see any KLA soldiers that day?

utterances.speaker: MERFIDETE SELMANI
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you. I have nothing further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Ms. Selmani, that concludes your evidence. Thank you for coming to the International Tribunal to give it. You are free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Ms. Romano, before we dealing with the next witness, there is one ruling which I want to give. It concerns the witness Mr. Radojkovic. Mr. Ryneveld, yesterday, asked us to consider whether that witness could give evidence by way of Rule 92 bis, that is by way of a written statement. I take it he would have conceded the cross-examination. But in any event, we've considered the matter and, given the nature of his evidence, we do not think it appropriate, and he should be called live. If you would pass that on, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: I will, Your Honour. And the other one -- I think the other witness that was mentioned, Karleusa, he will be taken live.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Your Honours, the next witness is K31, and I think we have an order for closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You have an order for closed session. Unless there are any other matters which should be dealt with in open session, we will go into closed session.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the witness take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. If you'd like to take a seat. I'm sorry, what?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said can I ask a question, Mr. May, before Ms. Romano starts the examination?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very briefly, because we need to get on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just briefly, yes. It has to do with Witness K31, because the opposite side, in its motion of the 29th of May, explained that it was a woman, (redacted), and it says that there was a sexual offence that was concerned. But when I read out the statement, this has nothing to do with a sexual assault or offence. So I'm asking you, why are we in closed session? Why is this witness a protected witness, and can you explain to me the reasons for your decision to hold a closed session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We will hear the statement read out, and if there is any issue arising, we will consider it.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Your Honours, maybe I will be able to clarify. In fact, there are two statements, and the sexual assault, it's contained in the second statement, and both were disclosed to the accused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Should I proceed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: I would like to show the witness this document. If the usher can distribute also. This is a one-page document containing the name of the witness and date of birth. Examined by Ms. Romano:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, can you please review the piece of document that is in front of you, and can you read, but without saying your name, can you confirm if this is your name and your date of birth.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K31
utterances.text: That is my name, my place of birth, and K31 written on it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. So during all the proceedings, you will be referred to by this number, K31. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K31
utterances.text: Yes, I understand you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: The Prosecution would like to submit the document into evidence and under seal.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit 266.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, you gave two statements to the Office of the Prosecutor. One on the 12th of March, 2002, and the second one on 12th of -- no, I'm sorry. The first one on 16 October 1999, and the second one on 12 March 2002. And -- yes?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K31
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in the second statement, you add information about what happened when you took your brother to the school (redacted) after he had been shot, and you left him at the hospital and stayed there. That's correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K31
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, you also attended a meeting with a representative of the Registrar, and at that meeting you had the opportunity to review both statements, and you had the statements read out to you in the Albanian language or you read them, and at that time, you confirmed that the contents of your statements, both, are correct and true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K31
utterances.text: Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Might the statements both be tendered into evidence, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We will have the exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit 267, which will be kept under seal.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: The witness is a (redacted) female Kosovo Albanian Muslim from the village of (redacted)in the municipality of (redacted). She's one of (redacted) children. Her father, (redacted), brother (redacted), and sister (redacted) were killed in (redacted) 1999 by Serb On (redacted) 1999, (redacted), the witness and her family was awoke by her mother who had heard gunfire nearby. They dressed and headed towards the mountains. A total of 16 people. They remained in the woods and after a time, (redacted) left to check if the road was clear. He was shot. The remainder of the group headed further into the woods and later that day, Serb troops approached them on foot. Her father and brother, in an attempt to escape, ran in different directions. The remainder of the group was shot at but none were -- but none injured. The witness recognised one of the soldiers. He went in the direction of her father, had taken. Later, she heard shots. As the soldiers approached, the witness's brother (redacted) and sister (redacted) were shot at. Her sister died ten minutes later. The group were allowed to leave. The witness carried her injured brother to the school in the village. They had to leave the dead girl where she died. From the school, the witness and her brother were taken to (redacted) in an APC. From there, they took another military vehicle to the hospital in Pristina. En route, she was threatened with being thrown into a river by a soldier in the APC. In this vehicle, she was handcuffed and repeatedly assaulted. At Pristina hospital, her brother was taken from her and she was taken to a dark room in the basement when -- where there was between 10 and 15 other young Kosovo Albanian women, one of whom informed her they had been brought there to be raped. A short time later, a soldier entered the room and selected the witness by torchlight, and he and two other soldiers took her to another basement room. In the room, she was forced to drink something bitter-tasting by one soldier while the other two were guarding the door. The drink affected her eyesight temporarily. In the room, she was viciously raped and assaulted by this first soldier, and when she was finished, he wiped his penis on her shirt, smearing her with blood. After this, one of the soldiers guarding the door entered the room and raped the woman twice. The third soldier entered and sat on her stomach. After this, she lost consciousness and awoke some time later. She went to the fifth floor of the hospital where she found her brother and managed to remain with him for the next two weeks, evading capture or being seen by hiding in the toilets and in her brother's bed. On leaving the hospital, she checked the room where the other women were held, but there was nobody there. The witness first travelled to her aunt's house (redacted) with her brother and then to her village (redacted) after 23 days of absence. She learned –

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Ms. Romano please slow down.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: I'm sorry. She learned the bodies of her father and brother were found close to where she last saw them. She states the reason she did not tell about the rape, that it was because of the shame associated with such an offence in the Muslim culture, and also she believed her family has suffered enough with the loss of her father, brother, and sister. Can the usher please show the witness Exhibit 18.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness --

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Can you put it on the ELMO, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, this is a set of photographs with men with uniform.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K31
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please point to the ones, if you can recognise any of them, that you saw in the hospital and the ones who took you to the room and raped you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K31
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you point to the Court, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K31
utterances.text: Number 3 and number 9. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many of them that were in the hospital?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K31
utterances.text: There were a lot of them in the hospital, but I would just count three.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: No further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic. Cross-examined by Mr. Milosevic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll begin at the beginning, and I'm not aware of the end because I haven't got that second statement, but I think that what I have heard suffices and that I can challenge it in its entirety. You gave a statement in 1999, and your second statement you gave in 2002; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K31
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you get the idea of giving another statement three years later?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's not three. One year. 1999 and 2000; it's a year later.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I heard 2002.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You are quite right. It was October 1999 and March 2002. So two years and a bit. Yes. Yes, Ms. Romano.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Your Honours, just to clarify, the second statement, the English version was disclosed on the 23rd of April this year --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: -- and the B/C/S on the 19th of June. But if the accused needs, we can provide a B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The accused is apparently prepared to go on as it is. Yes. You're quite right. Two and a half years later. So what you're being asked is how did it come about that you came to make the second statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This happened because when I gave the first statement, I was with my family, but -- and I had never told my family that I had been raped. I kept it to myself. And when they came to make a statement with my family, I didn't say. But when they came and took me to one side, I was able to talk about it when we were in private with them, because I was not able to tell anybody. I had to keep it to myself. And nobody in my family knew that I had been raped. But later, two and a half years later, I told only my mother.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please. Let's take a look at your first statement. Would you take a look at it, please. Just the second half of the statement, in fact. On the one but last page, you say: "My sister stayed in the forest where she was killed. I left with my mother, carrying my unconscious brother to the village school. From the school in (Redacted), they took us in a Serbian armoured personnel carrier." And then you say that: "Along the way, the soldiers stopped the APC on a bridge in front of the main road, and they took me out of the vehicle, and I was told to jump into the river, which I refused to do. One of the soldiers took his knife and put it on my throat. There was already blood on the blade. At the same time, the soldiers asked for my uncle. My answer was that I don't know anything about him. Then the soldiers tried to throw me by force into the river, but I succeeded to struggle by keeping my hands on the armature that was on the bridge. After a while, I was ordered back to the APC and I was taken to (redacted) with my brother." Therefore, a group of soldiers tried to throw you into the river, but as you were holding on firm to the armature, you succeeded in defending yourself, and they then took you back to the APC and took you to hospital with your brother. Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K31
utterances.text: That's right. If they had used greater force, they might have been able to throw me in the river. But because they didn't really want to do that, they used some very bad language and grabbed me by the hair. My hands were tied. After they didn't push me in the river, they tied my hands and put me in the APC.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they want to throw you into the river or did they not want to throw you in?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: She can't answer that. She can only say what actually happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Are you saying that this group of soldiers who wanted to throw you into the river didn't succeed in throwing you into the river because you were holding on to the rail? Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K31
utterances.text: I said I managed to hold on with what strength I had. But if they had tried harder, they could have thrown me in the water. But when they saw that I was resisting, they tied my hands and put me in the APC.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. It seems completely unbelievable, doesn't it, K31, that a group of soldiers wasn't able to throw you into the river when they had a mind to?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That is a comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, the question is: Does it seem to you to be quite unbelievable, K31, that a group of soldiers was not able to throw you into the river if they really wanted to? Doesn't it seem unbelievable?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It is a comment, Mr. Milosevic. This is what the witness said happened.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in this first statement of yours, after the paragraph that I read out, it says in the last sentence that your brother was treated 12 days. Now I heard from the summary read out by Ms. Romano that you say he was treated for 14 days. How long was your brother in hospital for? How did you -- how long did you spend in hospital with your brother? Was it 12 days or 14 days?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K31
utterances.text: Well, 12 to 14. It was something like that. Ten, 13; I can't say exactly how many days because this was three years ago, and maybe I've forgotten one day. I was traumatised. I could only say what I remembered when I gave my statement. It could be 12 or 13 or 14.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, all right. Three years later, you weren't traumatised. So you ought to be able to remember the number of days; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Does it really matter whether it was 12 or 14? There's no need to answer that. You've answered it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It does matter, Mr. May, because she's not telling the truth at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I'm going to read the penultimate paragraph now of your last sentence: "At Pristina hospital, I was alone with my brother. There was only water available, but nothing else. My brother was offered thin slices of bread, but I didn't get anything." Are you saying that they did not feed the patients in hospital, that they would withhold food to the patients, in Pristina at that, in the Pristina hospital?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K31
utterances.text: In Pristina hospital, they gave Serbs as much to eat as they could, but they gave me nothing, and they only gave my brother some thin slices. And we didn't even dare go outside to buy anything. And we survived in -- with water and a few biscuits I found in the corridor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. The main thing is for me to hear what you're saying, what you're asserting. And you're now asserting that in the Pristina hospital, they provided the Serbs with food but deprived the Albanians of food. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K31
utterances.text: They only gave Albanians two or three very, very thin slices of bread. And they took us Albanians high up to the fourth and fifth floors and kept the Serbs down below because the Serbs were frightened of the NATO bombing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Let's be quite precise here. They would just give you two thin slices of bread, to the Albanians, whereas they supplied the Serbs with normal amounts of food. And you only got two thin slices of bread at the hospital in Pristina. Is that what you're saying? Is that what you're claiming?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K31
utterances.text: They didn't give me anything. They merely gave my brother a little bit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right, for your brother, then. So to a patient in the hospital. And what you're saying is that they didn't give the Albanian patients any food at all except those two thin slices of bread. Is that what you're saying? At the Pristina hospital, at this point in time; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K31
utterances.text: Perhaps those of us had money they gave a bit more, even if we weren't Serbs, but they didn't give me anything at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just for clarification, Witness K31, at the hospital were you hiding at the time so that's the reason you didn't get any food?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was down in the basement, and I went upstairs, looking for my brother, and I stayed with him. And they saw me when I was staying with my brother, but they didn't give me anything to eat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And often I asked for food, but they wouldn't give me any.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, you say that they saw you and that they didn't give you food, and that often you even asked for food but they wouldn't give you any food. And a short while ago, you said that you were hiding all the time so that no one would see you so they wouldn't rape you again. Please, why are you lying?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. That's not a fair basis for putting the question. Have you told us the truth or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm telling the truth. I'm not lying to you. But I was not raped by any of the civilians, the doctors or people at the hospital. I was raped by people in uniform, and when they came, I hid.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Didn't you state a short while ago that you were hiding all the time, either in your brother's bed or in some toilets or I don't know where? That's what you said. That's what's recorded here in the transcript. And now you are saying that you were not hiding, that you asked them for food, that they saw you and that they didn't give you food, et cetera. So were you hiding or were you not hiding?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K31
utterances.text: I was only hiding from people in uniform.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, what were people in uniform doing in patients' rooms in hospitals? What were they doing in patients' rooms at all, men in uniform?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K31
utterances.text: These uniformed men changed every day and came regularly and patrolled all the wards and asked where we were from.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Are you claiming, then, that these soldiers in uniform - a short while ago you showed us one in a helmet - that these soldiers in uniform, in front of the doctors, because as you know, in the Pristina hospital doctors are Serbs, and Albanians and Muslims and others, so in front of the medical staff, the nurses, the orderlies, et cetera, they took you by the hand, took you to the basement in order to rape you? Is that what you claim happened at the Pristina hospital?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K31
utterances.text: No. It didn't happen like that. I wasn't grabbed by the doctors but by these people in uniform who brought me from (redacted) to Pristina. I was never bothered by the doctors. They checked my brother every now and then. But I was raped in the basement by young men in uniform. And when I came to, I didn't know what had happened. The doctors never bothered me at all, ever.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I never said that the doctors raped you. I asked you whether it is your claim that these men in uniform, before the eyes of the doctors and the nurses and the other staff in the overcrowded hospital, that these men took you downstairs into the basement to rape you. Is that your claim? Just say yes or no.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K31
utterances.text: No. They took me and took me down to the basement. The doctors were upstairs in their own quarters. But they took me to the basement. And I don't know where the doctors were, I didn't see them at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me just end what I've been quoting. It is sad that the other side resorts to such things. You say that your brother was given thin slices of bread. We established that. You claim that Albanians were not fed except for receiving thin slices of bread and that Serbs ate properly, that is your claim. And then you say: "Sometimes other patients gave me food as well, but on other occasions, I had just to take from the others. All Albanian patients were on the third floor --" and awhile ago you said on the fifth and fourth floor -- "and the Serbian patients were on the first and second floor because the personnel were afraid of NATO bombings. I could not leave the hospital because I was told that I would not be able to enter the hospital again." So if on the -- if you're on the second floor, you are safe from the bombing, and if you're on the third floor, then you'll get killed by the bombing. Is that something that was explained to you in the hospital? What kind of rule is this? Who explained this to you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K31
utterances.text: Nobody explained it to me, but I saw it myself that they took some people and took them up, and they -- and they kept the Serbs down below. And they told the Albanians, "You've got nothing to do down there, you get downstairs." And they didn't give us hardly any bread and they didn't give me any at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So do you claim that in the Pristina hospital, in the Pristina hospital Serbs and Albanians who were patients were divided according to floors and that on the floor where they were Albanian patients, there weren't any Serb patients, and where the Serb patients were, there weren't any Albanian patients on that floor? Is that what you're claiming? Just say yes or no.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K31
utterances.text: I'm telling you --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K31
utterances.text: -- but it's not like -- the Albanians were on the higher floors and the Serbs were down on the lower floors. And the doctors decided on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Forgive my interrupting you. It's a matter of policy. I've raised it before. This is an aggressive cross-examination without a positive case against a woman who is extremely vulnerable according to all the learning. I've raised before whether a man who has no apparent sympathy for victims should be allowed to cross-examine witnesses like this, and I must repeat our concern. We know imperfectly, others know better, the damage that is done and is sometimes intended to be done to witnesses in this position by this form of cross-examination. It is distasteful and, in my respectful submission, should be carefully monitored.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, we have to disagree. The accused is entitled to cross-examine. If he's doing it improperly, we'll stop him. Now, it may be distasteful to you. It may be distasteful to others that no word of remorse is mentioned, but that doesn't matter. As far as the trial is concerned, the accused is entitled, provided he doesn't overstep the mark, provided he didn't oppress the witness, he's entitled to put his case. You may not think there's very much in it, but nonetheless, he's entitled to put it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I shan't take any more of your time save to say of course I quite understand those concerns and the general principles that guide them. I am also acutely aware of the fact that learning about the associated problems of this type of witness has come more recently to my practice in such cases and therefore is something to which all of us may have only limited access, and I speak, therefore, out of an abundance of caution. Thank you for the time. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have to say that I would fully concur with what Mr. Nice said if I would even faintly believe that the witness were telling the truth. However, I'm convinced that the witness is not telling the truth. And in this statement that she gave two and a half years later, she added some complete falsehoods, as can be seen from other parallel statements --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That's a matter of argument. What comes out of it is this: You are entitled to cross-examine. But on the other hand, bear in mind, of course, the nature of the witness who you are cross-examining. And whether you accept it or not, many have been through very traumatic experiences, and that should be reflected in the way that they're treated in this court. That certainly is said. Yes, let's go on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, I respect the fact that many witnesses have lived through many terrible things during the war, certainly, but I don't see what this has to do with the accusations levelled against me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please. Now, let's look at the last paragraph of your statement. I started from the end, and I'll go back to other questions. So you left the hospital. You were there for 12 days or 14 days. That is no longer relevant. What is relevant is that in the hospital, there was segregation between the Albanians and the Serbs. That is to say that the Albanians were discriminated against. It is your claim that the Albanians were not fed, that the Serbs were fed, and so on and so forth, these few things. And that, practically, in this overcrowded hospital in Pristina during the war, you were raped.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Now, amongst other rules which you know, speech-making is not questioning. Now, what is the question of the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please. Where did they take you? They took you out of your brother's room; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K31
utterances.text: No, they didn't take me from my brother's room but they took me downstairs. I don't understand the --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where from? Where did they take you from? You were in the same room where your brother was. How many other patients were there in the room? Your brother was not the only patient in that room; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K31
utterances.text: Where my brother was, there were -- there were other people there, three other people. But I don't understand whether Milosevic is talking about when I came to the hospital or when I left. Because when they took me away, I wasn't with my brother.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, you say that you spent 14 days with your brother in the hospital, or 12 days at the hospital.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K31
utterances.text: That's right. But it was the first day when they took us to the yard. They took my brother upstairs, and they took me down to the basement. And I stayed all the night in the basement, and I went up looking for my brother, and I went up and found him upstairs. And I stayed 12 or 13 days, and then when we left, I went to the bus station, and we went together to my aunt's in (redacted).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Tell me, did you find your brother after the rape? Before the rape, you were not with your brother?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K31
utterances.text: We came to the hospital together and then they separated us. And my brother was sent upstairs, and I was sent downstairs, and I was raped. And I went upstairs and I looked for my brother and found him. And from then on, I was hiding from people in uniform because I was scared of being raped again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you said that you were hiding in your brother's bed and in toilets all that time; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: She's explained that she was hiding from the men in uniform. That was her explanation earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Let us look at this last paragraph now too. You say: "I arrived in (redacted) with my brother on the bus. There were only Serbs on the bus. When we got out of the bus, we went in the direction where my aunt lives. Along the road there were only Serbs. On the way, I was fixing the shoelace of my brother's shoe." That is to say, you bent down to do that; right? "At that moment, I was surrounded by about 20 Serb policemen and some civilians. I cannot tell their number. They asked me, What did you put on the ground? I said, Nothing. One from the crowd spoke to me and said if they found anything, they would kill both me and my brother. Then one civilian came and put a hand grenade on the ground while the rest of the crowd went away. The policeman talking to me said to me, Look what you did. You put the hand grenade on the ground." Did you put a hand grenade on the ground or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K31
utterances.text: No. On the road when I was going to my aunt, I tied my brother's shoelaces, and they came up to me and said, "What are you doing?" And I said, "I'm tying up my brother's shoes." And then a civilian put a grenade by my foot, and I told them that I -- I hadn't dropped this on the ground but they had planted it there. That's what I said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. All right. And then you say the following: "The man -- Look at what you did, you put the hand grenade on the ground. I said, He put it, pointing at the civilian, and then the policeman said in Albanian, And take your brother and go home. The man who put the grenade on the ground followed us to my aunt's house." So nothing happened to you then; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K31
utterances.text: No. Nothing happened to me then because we didn't take up the grenade. But they merely followed us. And when we went to my aunt's house, we went in and they followed me on the way.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters request the witness to speak more slowly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You're being asked, Witness K31, if you would speak more slowly, by the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It is your explanation that from time to time you had to move from your house to a safer place from when the offensive, as you had put it, started in January 1999. At that time, there was fighting between the KLA and the Serb army. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K31
utterances.text: The Serbian army, yes, but there was no KLA around there at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I had to find that page of yours. All right. Let's not waste any time. I can't -- all right. You went into the mountains. Who suggested that to you? Who suggested that you should go to the mountains? How did you decide to go to the mountains?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K31
utterances.text: We didn't decide to go to the mountains, but we live in the mountains. That municipality where I live, it's all very mountainous.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At that time you didn't see any Serbs; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K31
utterances.text: That day, in the morning? What day do you mean?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "At (redacted) in the morning on the (redacted) of May, my mother woke up hearing gunshots nearby." So that's the (redacted) of May.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K31
utterances.text: That's what happened in the early morning (redacted)of May [as interpreted]. My mother heard gunshots and woke up and got us up, and we went out and we joined a convoy and we -- we left. But my elderly relatives couldn't walk, and they just came up to us -- oh, I'm sorry. The Serbian forces just kept on drawing closer to us, and that's what happened. And at that moment, at (redacted), they killed my cousin. He asked for help and we saw him, but we didn't dare go to his aid.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Wait a minute, please. Let me just ask you another question. I asked you about whether you saw any Serbs on that day when you were fleeing into the mountains. So I'm reading page 6, on the first page of your statement [as interpreted], which says: "In the morning of the (redacted) my mother woke up hearing gunshots nearby. My mother woke all the family members and after we got dressed, we decided to go to the nearby mountain." Et cetera, et cetera. "We were leaving the house, we could hear gunshot bursts and shelling from the direction of the main road leading from Pristina to Skopje. As we were fleeing towards the mountain, we couldn't see any Serbs who we knew were close to the village." Now, I asked you whether you had seen any Serbs. Did you or did you not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K31
utterances.text: We only saw -- how shall I explain? We only saw the smoke of burning houses and heard people shouting. I didn't actually see the Serbs because they hadn't drawn close enough. But later, I did see them. I saw them 15 metres away, and they were talking in their language and insulting us, and I saw them in a line.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So did you see Serbs or did you not see Serbs, then, when you were fleeing into the mountains?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K31
utterances.text: We didn't go in the direction of the mountains, but that place is called the mountains. And we saw them, but they -- at that moment, they didn't see us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We're going to adjourn now for the break. Witness K31, could you remember during the break not to speak to anybody about your evidence until it's over, and that includes the members of the Prosecution team. Could you be back, please, in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, you have ten minutes left with this witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've lost a lot of time because I didn't know about the second statement, and as you were able to see, I had to clear up that second statement, Mr. May. So I have several more essential questions for this witness. And I checked it out --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. You can have ten minutes more. Twenty minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I just ask this: I heard during the break that there is no sound from this session or distorted image or anything else. According to your rules, how come this is a super protected witness with no sound, no image, distorted or otherwise, voice distortion or anything else?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's closed session, which means just that, closed. Completely closed. There is no sound, no image, nothing.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Then I'll continue with my questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Those who had their papers went abroad, the others, who didn't, went up into the mountains; is that true? That's what you explained; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K31
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I explained, but I said earlier it's at a place called (Redacted). It's not really a mountain, it's just a place called (redacted).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, you described the killing of your neighbour, (redacted). You didn't see who shot at him, did you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K31
utterances.text: Yes, I did see it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "While we were in the mountains, one of my neighbours, (redacted) (redacted), went away from the group to see if the road was free and when he had gone about 50 metres, I heard a shot and saw that he was hit by a bullet. And in my opinion, the bullet had been fired from a distance of about 200 metres. (redacted) fell to the ground," et cetera. So you didn't see who actually did the shooting, did you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K31
utterances.text: It wasn't one person, it was a whole group of people, of Serbs. I didn't see all of them. One of them I did see. I saw -- he had a bullet wound on his neck. But there was a group of people ten metres away, and we saw them pointing their automatic weapons, and there was firing. And we saw where the firing was coming from.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you saw that the shooting was coming from a distance of about 200 metres. That's what you said. Not 15 metres, 200 metres. And the people who were 20 metres away from you were a group of Serb soldiers. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K31
utterances.text: Later we were 20 metres from the soldiers, but there we were 50 metres away. And they shot. There wasn't just one of them, there was a whole group.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, but you said that the shooting, in your opinion, was coming from 200 metres away.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K31
utterances.text: Yes, I think it was about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. You also go on to explain that your brother was hit. However, you didn't see who shot at your brother, did you? That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K31
utterances.text: At (redacted) in the afternoon, I was with my father a bit farther up, to see what was going on at the edge, and we saw them armed, coming at us. And I said to my father and to my brother, "Get away, because they'll catch you when they come." So they went 10, 15 metres away, one in one direction, one in the other direction. And then he was -- he was hit. I saw it because there was a sort of fence there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, is it true that in that particular place at that particular time there was fighting going on between the army and the KLA?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K31
utterances.text: I don't think that's true. I saw Serbs there. I didn't see anyone else. They came and they burnt the houses down, and they murdered and marauded.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm talking about what you say happened in the forest. That means that there was fighting going on at that time; right? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K31
utterances.text: There was an offensive. Whether we wanted it or not, they were attacking and we were surrounded. They captured everyone and started murdering. That's what happened. There was nothing else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, all right. But is it true that it was the army precisely that helped you? The soldiers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K31
utterances.text: What, what army? Who helped us? No one helped us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll read out on page 4 of your statement, the middle paragraph there, says the following: "When I realised the situation of my brother and sister, I asked help from the Serb soldiers, but they would not reply to my request. They said that they couldn't help me because the terrorists might kill them." That's what you claim. That means that at that particular time, there was shooting going on, and that they weren't able to help you because they were afraid of the fire coming from the opposite side; right? Is that what it says? Is that so or is it not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K31
utterances.text: That's what they said. But they weren't killing terrorists, they were murdering us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Let me read the paragraph out until the end. "After that, I went to a middle-aged soldier, I grabbed his arm and took him to the place my sister and brother were lying." That's what it says. "This soldier spoke Albanian. After I took him to my brother, he called by radio another group which came ten minutes later and gave my brother first aid. They also advised me to take my brother to the school at(redacted) to another group which would then take my brother to Pristina for treatment." That's what you said. Therefore, at the beginning, they told you that they couldn't help you because they would be subject to gunfire and the terrorists might kill them. Then you grabbed a soldier by the arm, and he came and called someone up on the radio, administered first aid to your brother, sent your brother to the school at (redacted), and then took you to hospital in an APC. Does that mean from what you yourself say here both that there was fighting and that the army and soldiers helped you or does it not mean that? Just say yes or no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: She can't answer yes or no.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, it's not the way you say. They were killing people. How can they help people that they were trying to kill? There were no terrorists around.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I'm not saying anything. I'm not claiming anything, Madam Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. K31. I'm not saying anything. All I was doing was quoting from your own statement, and what I'm asking you emerges from your statement. These are all things that you yourself said, not me.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K31
utterances.text: I don't regret what I said. That's the way it was. There was radio communication to help us, but there were -- I saw what was going on. I saw exactly what was going on. You're making me nervous, you're trying to make me guilty of something, and I don't accept what you're insinuating.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment. Just a moment. Witness K31, there's no need to feel that. The accused is asking you some questions which arise from your statement, you see, in which you did say that an Albanian-speaking soldier called for help on the radio, and somebody came and gave your brother first aid. Is that right? Did that happen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's true. They gave first aid to my brother. A soldier gave him first aid. And at the same time, a group of soldiers murdered my sister and several other people, four or five other people. And we were surprised that my brother was given first aid, where at the same time they were murdering other people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was it obvious to you that the shooting was coming at your group and that the Serb soldiers were with you in that group? So it wasn't, in fact, coming from the Serb group, it was coming from the KLA which the Serbs were fighting.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K31
utterances.text: No, that's not true. There was no KLA there where we were, in our village, in that place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How do you explain, then, the fact that in the first part of that paragraph which I quoted, when you asked for help and they said they couldn't give you any help because they might be killed by the terrorists, just as you did not help your neighbour because you were afraid of being shot by a bullet, and in the same way they weren't able to help your brother at that particular moment because they were afraid of being shot by a bullet until you had solved the situation with the help of this soldier in another way. Is that right or not?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That's not a question. That's not a question. No need to respond to that. It's a comment if it's anything.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, all right, then.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true that that neighbour of yours - I don't want to have to search for his name again - was shot from a distance, in your opinion, of 200 metres? Is that right? And the soldiers who were with you and assisted your brother were there with you in the same place, in that same spot. They weren't able to help him from a distance, they had to tend to him and bandage his wounds there where you were on that spot, together with you; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K31
utterances.text: It's not exact, because we changed the place where we were. It wasn't the same place where we were with (Redacted). We were afraid of staying there and went a bit farther on, 50, 60 metres farther on. And when we went there, they really did give my brother first aid, that's true, but we were afraid -- they said they were afraid of the KLA. And I said, "There's no KLA here. Help my brother. There -- no one will do anything to you. No one will murder you here." Because I was sure that there was no KLA there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: They didn't seem to share your opinion, but let's move on with the questions.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K31
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So after that, anyway, they took you to the hospital; right? They helped you there on the spot and then took you to hospital; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K31
utterances.text: They sent us to the school in (Redacted) and then to the bridge, and then in (Redacted) to (Redacted) and then to the hospital. It was a long road. They were beating us all the time. I had -- my hands were tied up during all the journey.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This doesn't seem very probable to me, because in your statement you make no mention anywhere of the fact that they beat you. You just said that they wanted to throw you into the river. Now you say that they beat you throughout that journey, you and your brother to whom they had given assistance and help, is that what you're saying, on the road to the hospital?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K31
utterances.text: Down to the bridge they didn't beat me. But when they tried to throw me into the river, then from that time right to the hospital, they would beat me. They tore my hair. All -- they were really hard with me all the way to the hospital in Prishtina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And all that was going on in this APC, this armoured personnel carrier in which they were transporting you and your brother to hospital in?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K31
utterances.text: From the school in (Redacted) to (Redacted), we were in an armoured personnel carrier, but from (Redacted) to Pristina hospital, it was another vehicle. There were two vehicles involved.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, in which vehicle did they beat you? Tell me that, please. I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K31
utterances.text: They beat me in the vehicle where there was a bit of space to beat, whereas in the other vehicle, it was too enclosed, it was too narrow and there was no room to beat anyone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That means in that second vehicle in which they transported you from (Redacted) to the hospital; right? That's where they beat you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K31
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who was in that vehicle? Was it a van? Was it a small car? Was it a bus? What type of vehicle was it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K31
utterances.text: It was sort of like a kombi, but there was little room. It was like a van, but there was not too much room in it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was inside with you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K31
utterances.text: One had come from (Redacted), and others got in later, from reserve.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And so who beat you, then?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K31
utterances.text: The person who tried to throw me off the bridge into the river, who had bound my hands. The same person and others who were with him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It was that same man, was it? But you said that you reached the bridge in an APC and that they took you out of the APC at the bridge. Now you're saying that they beat you in the vehicle in which you went from (Redacted)to Pristina. How could that same man who was in the transporter be found in this vehicle going to Pristina from (Redacted)? Answer me that, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K31
utterances.text: Okay, I will answer you. The person who had tried to throw me off the bridge, he had a long beard, and he kept making gestures, like this. But it was very, very -- we were very close. He had an automatic weapon. And when we got into a bigger vehicle, there were three people in it. They tried to rip off my clothes with their knives, with all three of them, but the one with the beard was right beside me all the time. I was crying all the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So they wanted to rip your clothes off in the vehicle that you were riding in together with your brother, who was wounded, from (Redacted) to the hospital in Pristina; is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K31
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, that's the way it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So your wounded brother was in the vehicle, you were in the vehicle, and these three men. Were they soldiers, policemen? What were they? They were soldiers; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K31
utterances.text: I was so horrified, but I did see police and military uniforms, and they were armed. They were really fully armed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, did I understand you correctly to say that the man with the beard who was with you was both in the APC and later on in this other vehicle from (Redacted) to Pristina? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K31
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. To Pristina. And the first one who raped me at the hospital, he was there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that's the one with the beard; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K31
utterances.text: Yes. And during the offensive where they killed my father and my brother, he had a bandanna around his head, but then he'd taken -- and it said "Massacre" written on it, but later on, he took it off.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, this will be your last question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did I understand you correctly? The man who was in the APC, within the team in the APC and who took you to the bridge and wanted to throw you into the river and brought you to the school in (Redacted)in the APC, he left the APC, got into the other vehicle with you, beat you on the way, and when they took you to the hospital with your brother, that same man found you and raped you. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K31
utterances.text: He was with me all the time, right behind me. Not from the site with the APC. We went to the school within half an hour, that first half hour, and there was no problem there. We didn't know what was going on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Wladimiroff, have you any questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: One thing, Your Honour. Questioned by Mr. Wladimiroff:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, do you speak Serbian?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K31
utterances.text: No, I don't. A little, a very little bit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you read Serbian letters, Cyrillic letters?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K31
utterances.text: Not really. A little bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Thank you. That's all I ask.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: I will be brief, Your Honours. I have just two or three matters. Re-examined by Ms. Romano:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you need some water, Witness?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K31
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, you heard the accused saying that everything you said in the second statement about the rape that was committed against you, it's not true. So you heard the accused saying that you made up everything. What would be your reaction to that accusation, to that suggestion that you made all this up? Can you tell the Judges what would be your reaction?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K31
utterances.text: I would say that's true. Yes, I did experience that myself. And you may not -- other people may not believe it, but I was a virgin. I'd never had relations with others. And now I'm terribly frightened of people with beards. You can believe me or not, whether you want to or not, but that's what I went through. And if it wasn't the truth that I was telling you, I wouldn't have bothered to come here to tell you anything but the truth.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K31
utterances.text: Really, I insist. That's really the truth.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, it took almost three years for you to tell your mother and also to give the statement about the rape. During all this time, you did not tell anybody. Why is that? Why is that so difficult for a girl like you to tell people about what happened to you, especially in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K31
utterances.text: It's terrible to speak about such things in Kosova. You -- it's not -- Albanian women are not looked upon well if they -- they have to suffer in silence. I had -- I was frightened that if people knew that I had been raped, that no one would ever marry me or want to marry me, and that's why I didn't mention it. The first time they asked, there were local interpreters there, but I told them about it, and they told me not to worry about it. But there were children around, and people were worried about me, and I didn't know exactly what to do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do people not understand or help?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K31
utterances.text: Well, maybe there are some people who are helpful, but it's hard to say. You can never really know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, do you see any reason for you to lie, to create something like this, in light of the fact of what you've just said?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K31
utterances.text: No. I have no reason to lie. Why would I want to lie? I experienced these things, and I want to tell them as they happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Your Honours, in light of the observations made by Mr. Milosevic about the proceedings in closed session, I respectfully request the Chamber to remind Mr. Milosevic about the proceedings that involve a closed session regarding communications outside the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He knows what the rules are. He said he would obey them.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: No. I said that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: There should be no disclosure.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Exactly. I just said that he seemed to not understand what was happening and why there was no sound and everything. This is not the first time that a closed session had taken place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He knows now.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: That's all, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Witness K31, thank you for coming to the Tribunal to give your evidence. You are free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would you be so kind, Mr. May, as to explain to me, please, that is to say a moment ago Ms. Romano said that this is not the first time we've had a closed session, and that's quite true, but the first time we did have a closed session was, I if recall -- this is the first time we had a closed session with a witness. Up 'til now, they had face or voice distortion, but we didn't have a closed session for witnesses. So I don't understand why it is necessary to have a completely closed session for this particular witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's not so, Mr. Milosevic, because we have had other female witnesses in the same situation as this particular witness and in closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: K15, K14, K20, K16; all those witnesses.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I completely -- does that mean that these transcripts are not made public either, the LiveNote from the closed sessions are not made public either?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That's right. They're not public. They're closed. And you know the reason in this case why they are closed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Your Honours, the next witness is K24 and is also in closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let the witness take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you'd like to take a seat.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Your Honours, can I have this document shown to the witness. It's a one-page document with the name and date of birth of the witness. Examined by Ms. Romano:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, could you please review the paper that is in front of you, and can you tell with a yes or no if this is your name and your date of birth.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K24
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you see a number on this sheet, "K24"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K24
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Throughout these proceedings, you will be referred to as you K24. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K24
utterances.text: Yes, I understand that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Might the document be tendered into evidence under seal?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit 268.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, you gave a statement to the Office of the Prosecutor on the 22nd of November, 1999. Is that correct? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K24
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you attended a meeting on the 15th of July, 2002, where you reviewed that statement before a presiding officer of the Registrar and members of the Prosecutor, and you confirmed that that statement is correct and true; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K24
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in that opportunity, you also made an addendum to that statement, correcting some minor issues, and also you were shown photographs and you explained each one of the photographs; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K24
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: The Prosecution formally submits the statement and the addendum into evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit 269 and 269A for the redacted version.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: The witness is a (Redacted) Kosovo Albanian woman whose statement deals with events in the spring 1999 when she was staying at her parents' house (Redacted) municipality, a village occupied entirely by Kosovo Albanians. (Redacted) (Redacted). Early one morning at the end of March, beginning of April, VJ soldiers arrived and surrounded the village, and for safety reasons, the witness and some other women and children, numbering 22 in total, hid in a house on a hill further up the village. The men, including her father and brother, fled to the mountains. The following morning, soldiers arrived at the house where the women and children were sheltering. The women and children were searched and robbed and their IDs confiscated. They were then ordered to walk to (Redacted)and were escorted by armed VJ soldiers. However, before arriving at (Redacted) they were intercepted by a VJ truck and ordered to return to (Redacted). The women and children were held at a house in (Redacted)for three days. During this time, they were searched and robbed again by a Serb-speaking woman named Mirdita, who assisted the soldiers. The women and children from (Redacted)were then ordered to walk to the mosque in (Redacted). The witness heard various reasons why they had to go to (Redacted). One soldier said it was to protect them from NATO bombing. Mirdita said, "They're asking for a group of you there," but gave no further explanations. When they reached(Redacted), the soldiers directed the women and children to a house near the mosque where they were held in a cowshed.The VJ soldiers who escorted them handed them over to the soldiers with tiger badges on their arms.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Ms. Romano please slow down. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: I apologise and I will slow down. The women were robbed and threatened before being taken out in groups to be checked. The witness was told by her cousin, aunt and sister how they had been forced to strip naked and the soldiers touched their breasts and vagina. She also testifies that (Redacted) (Redacted), the soldiers also forced her to strip and touched her breasts and vagina. On two separate occasions, soldiers removed their lower garments, and the witness believes that they wanted to rape her. On the first occasion, the witness fainted, and on the second occasion, the soldier threatened to cut her (Redacted) but did not rape her. The witness describes the physical and emotional condition of women who were "checked" and the comments they made. The witness believes that some of the other women and girls had been raped. The soldier removed five younger women and three older women from the group. One of the soldiers made a comment in Albanian, implying that the women were going to die. The witness believes the older women were killed immediately, as she heard three shots from outside. The five younger women, one of whom was the witness's sister, failed to return. The witness subsequently discovered that all eight women had been found dead (Redacted), near the shed where they had all been held. (Redacted) (Redacted). In the addendum made by the witness, there are photographs of the wells and the place where the witness was held, and she describes and identifies all the witness [sic]. Unless the Judges want, I will not show the witness the photos.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No, but I think formally they should be exhibited.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Yes. They are part of the addendum. If you want to exhibit them separately --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let them be exhibited formally. We'll need some copies for the Court. They can be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit number 269B, to be kept under seal.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: There are copies, although black and white, attached to the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Are they also part of the (Redacted)binder?

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: No, they are not. The (Redacted) binder contains only the autopsy -- the forensic report.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: It may assist the Court that it is a part of the (Redacted) binder, under tab 7.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: No, I'm sorry, the tab was deleted.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Tab 8.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: It was also -- I think it was removed. When the binders were disclosed to the amici and the accused, they contained the photos, but after, according to a ruling, we removed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: And we are formally introducing to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Whatever. It's right that they should be exhibited and exhibited separately now. Yes. Now, Mr. Milosevic, have you got any questions of this witness?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do, Mr. May. Cross-examined by Mr. Milosevic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Tell me, please, first of all - I did not understand from this statement - you say that you were in your parents' house in the village of (Redacted). Which municipality is this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K24
utterances.text: This village is in the municipality of (Redacted).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. You say that you left the village after the bombing started, and you do not know on which day or date the bombing started and you left.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K24
utterances.text: No, I don't know the date.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It was my understanding that you left the village because you thought that you were safer if you'd leave the village. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K24
utterances.text: We left and we went up above, and we left our house behind to take shelter further up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. You don't know the time, and you don't know -- you say that was after NATO had started the bombing in 1999. After how much time? Was it a day or two or five days or a month after NATO started bombing? Could you give us just an approximation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K24
utterances.text: No. I don't know how long after the start of the bombing it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. You came to your relative's house, and he went into the mountains the same night; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K24
utterances.text: I didn't understand the question. Could you repeat it, please?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I asked you when you went to the mountains, when you left the village, you came where? You came to your relative's house, if I understood you correctly.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K24
utterances.text: That's right. We left my own family home and went up to my cousin's to take shelter, for security reasons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where did this relative of yours live?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K24
utterances.text: A few metres further up, above our house. About one kilometre.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. That means that you just moved into the neighbourhood. You moved into the house next door. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K24
utterances.text: Yes. It was within the same village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And why did you think that you were safer in the house next door rather than in your own house if it's only a few metres away?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K24
utterances.text: Because we were facing up to the Yugoslav army. So to avoid them, we went up the hill, took shelter some distance away.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what about the members of your family, your husband and the others? Were they members of the KLA?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K24
utterances.text: No. My father, who was there with my brothers, were all civilians and went out, took shelter in (Redacted).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On page 3 in the Serbian version, in the first line, you say in your statement: "My father and my other brothers went into the mountains to hide. (Redacted)." (Redacted), right? That's where the KLA forces were. Are you now saying something different, or do you abide by what is written in this statement of yours?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K24
utterances.text: My husband did not fight. He was only on the KLA's list of volunteers. He didn't have a uniform or weapons. He was a civilian again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ms. K24, I did not present a claim of my own. I quoted your statement. The sentence is a very short one, and it reads: "(Redacted) (Redacted)." That's it, from the first capital letter until the full stop at the end. So is that uncontested or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K24
utterances.text: I can only say that my husband was a KLA volunteer on the list, but he didn't have a uniform or a weapon, and I don't know what else to say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And on page 8 of your statement, in connection with the description of this friend of yours, a person, I don't know how to call her, Mirdita, she was also KLA. It says in the penultimate paragraph -- the one before the penultimate paragraph, actually: "I met with my husband two months after the peace agreement was signed. He fought in the KLA for six months in (Redacted)." And then further on, he says to you that he saw Mirdita in (Redacted) before what happened in (Redacted), uniform, that she cooperated with the army, et cetera, et cetera. So in two places in the statement, you say that your husband was with the KLA, in the KLA. I'm asking you quite precisely now: Did you move from your own house to the house next door because you thought that the police that knew that your husband was a member of the KLA would come to your house to look for him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K24
utterances.text: No. We didn't flee for that reason. We went away to protect ourselves. We had children, (redacted); we just had to leave that house and go to another one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. When you were with the army, you described that in your statement. You say that they were correct when dealing with you. And you say: "For three days, things were quite all right." That's the beginning of page 4 in the Serbian version. "They brought us food, the soldiers did, milk, cheese, whatever else they could find in different houses, everything they could find. They brought us tea and sugar, and there was a furnace there, but we could use it only for heating, however, we could not use it for baking bread. We had to go upstairs. The Yugoslav army soldiers allowed us to do this but not every time we asked," et cetera. So were they correct towards you in every way?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K24
utterances.text: No. It was only one day when they took us to that house. They gave us food and drink, and I never saw them any more.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I beg your pardon. Let me just remember the number. Oh, yes. Ms. K24, I quoted your own statement to you a little while ago, and you said, "For three days we were really fine," and then you say the rest. I don't want to take up my time quoting it again. And then you say that you were told by them to go to (redacted), but they said that to you so that you could hide in the mosque, because NATO may bomb and kill you; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K24
utterances.text: Yes. In -- for three days we were together with them in (redacted).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And after that, you left. Did you go to hide in the mosque when they told you to hide in the mosque? Did you think that they wished you well, that they wished to protect you because they assumed that NATO would not bomb a mosque?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K24
utterances.text: No, I don't think they wished us well. We only thought that something worse awaited us. And that's what happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, but I understand your statement to say that these soldiers, these men that you were with, did nothing to you during those few days while they helped you and when they sent you to seek shelter in the mosque. It was my understanding of what you wrote here that they took care of you. They tried to help you. They tried to protect you from the bombing, et cetera. So who did something bad to you, they or somebody else?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K24
utterances.text: The soldiers said that they would take us to the (redacted)mosque to protect us, but they didn't take us there. They took us and left us in the hands of criminals.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please explain this to me, clarify it for me: My understanding of your statement was that the soldiers escorted you to (redacted)for your own safety and security and that then you remained in (redacted). What do you mean they left you in the hands of criminals? You were not arrested to be handed over to someone. You stayed in (redacted); is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K24
utterances.text: The three soldiers who took us to (redacted)left us in a yard. One of them went and called the criminals.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He went to call the criminals, this soldier who brought you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K24
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were these criminals some kind of thieves, bandits? What did they look like?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K24
utterances.text: They mistreated us. They insulted us. They swore at us. And then they drowned my sister and my mother-in-law.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
